Some attention heads look congruent, pointing at positions in earlier cycles that line up with t+1 mod p. Layer 11 head 1 and layer 15 head 7 both show this clearly, with layer 15 head 7 also acting as a strong induction head. I'm now checking layer 15 head 5.

I'm checking the remaining heads in layers 19 and 23, which show congruent attention in the 0.23 to 0.58 range. I also want to test whether the same heads attend to positions matching t mod p, since a much stronger match for t+1 would mark them as true induction heads.

I'm weighing whether to ablate the induction heads at all, since they also copy useful spans like equations. A better target may be the direction that signals "I'm already repeating," and how that relates to the decision to emit </think>. With only eight forward passes, the aim is to get the model out of its loops, because most finished answers are already correct and the reference answer usually appears before the loop starts.

I'm working out how likely the model is to escape the loop: with the per-token loop probability this high at temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 would keep only the repeated token, so once the loop is entrenched, exiting it is effectively impossible.

I'm now looking at how to break the loops: the model locks into an exact repetition, and at temperature 0.6 with top_p 0.95 a confident loop leaves no room for exit, so I need to find where alternatives like "</think>" could still get enough probability to escape.

I'm weighing a targeted intervention now: scaling down the output contribution of specific attention heads through their o_proj columns, since each query head maps to one KV group and its slice of the output can be scaled on its own. I'm also considering a separate route, finding a direction that encodes "I'm already repeating" and seeing how it connects to the decision to emit </think>.

I'm considering whether to attack the repetition itself, perhaps by finding a feature in the residual stream that tracks when the text is looping and wiring it to boost the </think> logit. That would be conditioned on the failure rather than the problem, though it feels like an artificial addition. I'm also looking at whether the model already has anti-repetition or copy-suppression heads that are simply too weak over long contexts. A clear signal to check is the "Wait" token, which accounts for about 93% of loop cycles.

I'm considering whether the "Wait" tokens, which show up in most loop cycles, come from a set of MLP neurons that push toward re-verification. Scaling those down might cut the loops, but "Wait" also does real self-correction, so the trade-off is unclear.

Next I'm weighing which intervention is most likely to pay off: the loops appear to be about failing to stop rather than failing at the math, since the reference answer already shows up before most loops begin. The verification re-check that starts each loop, then gets copied verbatim by the induction heads, seems like the place to look.

I'm weighing whether the model can escape its loops at all, since without the induction heads reinforcing the repetition it might keep varying the "Wait" re-checks without ever emitting </think>.

I'm planning a paired comparison: one generation pass of 256 problems at 32k tokens, which should show whether an edit moves accuracy well above the 8.4% baseline. Before running that, I need to find the edit itself, and cheap teacher-forced passes on the loop texts can test candidate changes first.

I'm planning to measure the edit with teacher-forced passes on about 80 loop texts, since their onset sits near 6.5k tokens. I'll compare the loop-continuation logprob, the reference-solution logprob as a math check, and the probability of </think> at the decision points.

I'm planning the teacher-forced passes now: first a baseline pass of the original model over loop texts, finished texts, and reference solutions to get per-token logprobs and top-k, then a pass with each candidate edit on the same set so the two can be compared. I'll keep an eye on the memory cost of saving hidden states across that many tokens.

I'm laying out the next steps: first a generation run on 128 problems with two samples each at 32k tokens to see whether accuracy moves, then refining the edit and confirming on held-out problems. Before using any of those passes, I want to work out the weight-level picture of the gated full-attention layers, since that determines which candidate edits are even available.

I'm checking the attention layer's gate and query split in Qwen3-Next: each head's rows are divided into a query slice and a gate slice, and the gated output goes through o_proj. To dampen one query head, I'd scale its slice of o_proj's columns, so I want to confirm the tensor names for a full attention layer first.

I'm weighing which heads to target: layer 15 head 7 looks like the strongest induction head in the loops, with layer 11 head 1 and several layer 23 and layer 19 heads close behind. The worry is that those same heads handle ordinary copying in normal reasoning, so damping them could also hurt arithmetic. Linear attention layers can copy too, so the effect might be partly offset.

I'm thinking about whether the induction heads' attention to every earlier loop cycle could be what compounds the self-reinforcement, since each prior cycle adds to the congruent mass. I'm also checking whether a repetition-tracking direction in the residual stream might connect to the decision to emit </think>, though that would be tied to the failure rather than the cause.

I'm checking whether the "Wait" token at the start of each loop cycle is what locks the model in, since its probability near 1 would mean the loop is effectively sealed. The open question is whether suppressing "Wait" when many have already appeared could give the model a way out.

I'm checking how often "Wait" appears in the finished samples and what the context looks like right where each loop begins. A quick check of the tokens that open each cycle should show whether the lock-in is concentrated there.

I'm considering whether the presence penalty of 1.5 could be driving the loops: as common tokens get penalized, the model may be shifted toward rare, odd tokens like the deeply indented "            *   " pattern. Each distinct whitespace count is a different token, so fresh ones would get the penalty bonus, which might explain the odd formatting.

I'm now designing a first edit experiment: teacher-forced passes over loop texts with the induction heads scaled down, to test whether the loop continuation's logprob drops from its near-zero value.

I'm now testing whether the loops can be broken by scaling down the induction heads, since a teacher-forced pass can check the loop continuation's probability before any full generation run. Each edit candidate costs one pass, so I'll have to pick the candidates carefully, and I'm considering whether several edits could be combined in one pass.

I'm planning the next passes: a teacher-forced run on the original model over loop and finished texts to collect top-k and hidden states at decision points, then a 128-problem generation run with two samples each at 32k tokens for candidate edit A to measure the accuracy difference.

Now I'm weighing whether to dampen the top induction heads, since they would be the first causal test, though they may also be the heads doing ordinary copying in arithmetic.

I'm looking at whether a residual-stream direction tied to "ready to answer" could explain why the looping samples never reach finish-intent. The idea is to compare that direction at the points where the model picks between "Wait" and "</think>" after stating an answer, to see whether a doubt-like feature is what drives the choice to re-check.

I'm recalling that work on reasoning models points to excessive "Wait" reflection as a driver of overthinking loops, with suppressing those tokens or steering away from them as known remedies. SEAL is the example I have in mind: it found a steering vector from middle-layer states that separate reflection from execution, subtracted it during decoding, and got better accuracy with less redundant reflection.

Adding a constant steering shift to the residual stream would normally need a bias term, and these layers don't seem to have one. So a direct SEAL-style vector subtraction isn't available as a plain weight edit, and I'd have to look for a nearly constant neuron to exploit instead.

I'm considering a directional ablation: projecting a "reflection" direction out of the outputs of several layers' down_proj or o_proj weights, rather than adding a constant vector, since there are no biases to carry one.

I'm looking at projecting a "reflection" direction out of the residual-stream writers, the o_proj and down_proj matrices, with a strength knob so it's a partial ablation. The open question is whether removing the model's ability to represent reflection would stop the "Wait" loops or also damage useful self-checking, so I want to find the direction from hidden states at the points where "Wait" starts.

I'm planning to collect hidden states from a dedicated teacher-forced pass over about 100 texts, since the existing two-text dump is probably too small to estimate a direction. Storing several layers at full token count would run to several gigabytes, so I'd keep the layer count and token count modest.

I'm weighing how temperature 0.6 with top-p 0.95 behaves inside a loop: the top token's probability is so high that nucleus sampling keeps only that token, so the output is effectively deterministic. The loop only breaks if some position flattens enough that the top token falls below 0.95, which would require a small logit gap between candidates.

I'm working through the arithmetic of the loop: a top token has to fall below 0.95 at T=0.6, which means the alternative would need to sit within about 1.8 nats of it. The measured cycle logprob of -0.003 per token says the gaps are far larger than that, so nucleus sampling never gets a chance to pick anything else.

I'm weighing induction-head damping against the reflection-direction approach: the first cycle's high confidence suggests copying from a single earlier occurrence, but damping copying could also hurt the arithmetic accuracy I need to preserve. The literature on steering away from reflection points toward better accuracy, so I'm leaning that way, though I still want to check the actual data before settling on either edit.
